rows.title: Securing Model Context Protocol Servers: Security Assessment and a Lightweight Wrapper-Based Hardening Approach
rows.authors: Anitha Dhananjeyan; Vishnu Kiran Dabbara; Amit Kumar Mishra; Fatiha Djebbar
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to interact with external tools, resources, file systems, and platform features. Although this improves interoperability in agent-based systems, improperly configured MCP servers may expose serious security risks, including unauthenticated tool invocation, excessive file access, arbitrary command execution, prompt injection, token replay, response leakage, and denial-of-service behavior. The current work presents a controlled security assessment of an insecure MCP server and evaluates a lightweight FastAPI-based security wrapper that hardens

rows.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) at First Glance: Studying the Security and Maintainability of MCP Servers
rows.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
rows.authors: Mohammed Mehedi Hasan; Hao Li; Emad Fallahzadeh; Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur
rows.abstract: Although Foundation Models (FMs), such as GPT-4, are increasingly used in domains like finance and software engineering, reliance on textual interfaces limits these models’ real-world interaction. To address this, FM providers introduced tool calling—triggering a proliferation of frameworks with distinct tool interfaces. In late 2024, Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to standardize this tool ecosystem. With SDK downloads surpassing twenty five million per week and 86% of enterprises using models supporting MCP tools, MCP is rapidly emerging as a de facto industry standard.

rows.title: mcp-safeguard: An Automated Security Scanner for Model Context Protocol (MCP) Servers
rows.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
rows.abstract: mcp-safeguard is an open-source security scanner purpose-built for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem. It detects Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), credential exposure, prompt injection, tool poisoning, and security misconfigurations across MCP server implementations, with 40+ CVSS-scored detection rules across four vulnerability classes. The scanner was used to identify and responsibly disclose SSRF vulnerabilities in official MCP server implementations published by Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google.

rows.title: MCP Servers in Agentic AI - Architecture, Adoption, and Security of the Model Context Protocol
rows.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, has emerged as a widely adopted open standard forconnecting large language model (LLM) applications to external tools, data sources, and services. By standardizing the interfacebetween an AI host application and the servers that expose capabilities to it, MCP has been described as a USB-C-like connectorfor agentic AI, replacing bespoke, one-off integrations with a single, reusable protocol. rows.title: Security Posture Evaluation of Model Context Protocol Servers Against Prompt Injection
rows.venue: IEEE International Symposium for Design and Technology in Electronic Packaging (SIITME)
rows.authors: Gabriela TOD-RĂILEANU; Sabina-Daniela Axinte; Ana-Maria Dincă; Ioan C. Bacivarov
rows.abstract: This study presents a security-oriented evaluation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard enabling large language models (LLMs) to interface with external tools through structured interactions. The experiment was deployed in a controlled environment using an open-source MCP server with basic file manipulation tools. A set of prompt injection tests was designed to probe the system's ability to handle adversarial instructions, ambiguous input, and encoded payloads. rows.title: First Comprehensive Security Audit of the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem: 728 Servers Analyzed
rows.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an emerging standard for LLM-tool integration seeing rapid adoption in production environments. Despite its importance to AI infrastructure security, no comprehensive security baseline exists for the ecosystem. We conducted the first systematic security audit of 728 publicly documented MCP servers, applying a 7-category exploitability-focused methodology across input validation, information disclosure, rate limiting, CORS configuration, tool output safety, resource isolation, and known vulnerabilities. rows.title: Same Name, Different Server: A Security Census of Silent Drift in the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the common interface through which large language model applications reach external tools, and its public registry now distributes thousands of community-built servers with little of the vetting infrastructure that mature package ecosystems have accumulated. This paper reports a census of that ecosystem. rows.title: Freie Titelübersetzung: How secure is your AI agent? Security Analysis of Model Context Protocol (MCP) Servers with and without Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to interact with external tools in a standardised way, facilitating the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents that can perform complex tasks autonomously on behalf of the user. However, MCP servers introduce new attack surfaces that can be exploited via prompt injection. This thesis analyses the risks posed by MCP servers and evaluates whether Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) can effectively mitigate these risks without causing unmanageable disruption. rows.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions
rows.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
rows.authors: Xinyi Hou; Yanjie Zhao; Shenao Wang; Haoyu Wang
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an emerging open standard that defines a unified, bi-directional communication and dynamic discovery protocol between AI models and external tools or resources, aiming to enhance interoperability and reduce fragmentation across diverse systems. This paper conducts a systematic study of MCP from both architectural and security perspectives. We first define the full lifecycle of an MCP server, comprising four phases (creation, deployment, operation, and maintenance), further decomposed into 16 key activities that capture its functional evolution. rows.title: A Taxonomy of Runtime Faults in Model Context Protocol Servers
rows.authors: Joshua Owotogbe; Indika Kumara; Antonio Ken Iannillo; Willem Jan van den Heuvel
rows.abstract: MCP (Model Context Protocol) enables LLMs (Large Language Models) to interact with external tools and data sources via a standardized protocol. Its rapid adoption in tool-augmented Artificial Intelligence (AI) workflows has introduced new reliability challenges, such as configuration parameters that are accepted but not enforced at runtime, leading to unintended default behavior, whose runtime fault characteristics remain empirically unexamined. rows.title: Software Supply Chain Hygiene of Model Context Protocol Servers: An Empirical Study
rows.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
rows.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has, within roughly eighteen months of its release, become the dominant mechanism by which large language model agents discover and invoke external tools. Public registries already list tens of thousands of MCP servers, and a growing body of security research has begun to characterize the protocol-level risks this introduces, including authentication gaps, prompt-injection-driven tool invocation, and taint-style code execution vulnerabilities in server implementations.
